analysis.one_liner: Lets either party to a product sales-and-service contract reject forced arbitration after a dispute arises.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote; it died in a House Judiciary subcommittee despite a Republican sponsor and 15 bipartisan cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Contracts between manufacturers and the businesses that resell and service their products often require any dispute to be settled by binding arbitration, with no day in court. This bill would have let either side, once a dispute actually arose, reject arbitration in writing and go to court instead. It also would have required arbitrators to give a written explanation of the factual and legal basis for any award. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Commercial and Administrative Law Subcommittee, where it died without any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that buy products for resale and are authorized to repair and service them — such as franchised dealerships and independent repair shops. When a manufacturer disputes a contract term or owes them money, they could refuse arbitration and argue their case in court, where procedures are public and precedents exist. Consumers benefit only indirectly, through dealers who can hold manufacturers accountable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Franchised dealers and independent repair businesses

how_it_helps.text: Each party to a covered sales and service contract could, after a controversy arises but before arbitration begins, reject arbitration in writing and take the dispute to court [S3].

The bill defines covered contracts as those where a manufacturer, importer, or distributor sells a product for resale to an ultimate purchaser and authorizes the buyer to repair and service it — the classic manufacturer-to-dealer arrangement [S3].
When arbitration is used anyway, the arbitrator must provide a written explanation of the factual and legal basis for the award, instead of a bare result [S3].
The change would apply only to contracts entered into, amended, renewed, or extended after enactment, so existing contracts would keep their arbitration clauses until renegotiated [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, importers, and distributors that wrote mandatory arbitration clauses into their dealer networks would lose their ability to keep disputes out of court, facing public litigation instead. Arbitration providers would handle fewer disputes, and arbitrators would face new paperwork requirements.

drawbacks.text: Mandatory binding arbitration is often faster and cheaper than litigation, and small dealers might sometimes do better in arbitration than in court, where legal costs are higher and manufacturers have deeper pockets [S3].
Requiring arbitrators to write a full factual and legal explanation for every award adds time and cost to the process the bill leaves intact [S3].
Because the bill only covers manufacturer-to-reseller contracts, it would do nothing for consumers facing arbitration clauses in their own sales or service contracts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have shifted real power from large manufacturers to smaller dealers by ending one-sided forced arbitration in their contracts, at the cost of giving up arbitration's speed and lower cost in some cases. Its written-explanation requirement was a modest transparency improvement. But it was narrow: it did not touch consumer arbitration clauses, and it died without ever being debated, so none of its effects materialized.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee from November 1997 until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Sonny Bono introduced the bill on November 7, 1997, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S5].
On November 18, 1997, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill ended the 105th Congress with 15 cosponsors — 11 Republicans and 4 Democrats — but never reached a committee vote or the House floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers, importers, and distributors came out ahead: by never facing a vote, the bill died quietly, and their mandatory arbitration clauses over dealer and service-network disputes remained unchallenged in federal law. Dealers and repair businesses gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Manufacturers keeping arbitration clauses over dealers

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call breakdown exists, but sponsorship was bipartisan: a Republican sponsor with 15 cosponsors split 11 Republicans and 4 Democrats.

industries.industry: Vehicle and equipment manufacturers, importers, and distributors
industries.note: These companies use mandatory arbitration clauses in their sales-and-service contracts with dealers and repair shops to keep contract disputes out of public courts. The bill would have let either side reject arbitration after a dispute arose, exposing their contract practices to litigation. Their gain from the bill's failure is dealers' continued lack of a court option.

industries.industry: Franchised dealers and independent repair and service businesses
industries.note: These small businesses would have gained the right to take disputes with manufacturers to court instead of binding arbitration, and to get written reasoning whenever arbitration went forward. This is a small-business benefit; ordinary consumers benefit only indirectly.
Fewer disputes would be forced into arbitration, reducing case volume, while the arbitrators who did serve would have to produce written factual and legal explanations for awards.
